newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Better times seen for Europe's forest industry.
newsitem.headline: Better times seen for Europe's forest industry.

text.p: The worst seems to be over for Europe's forest industry, which was hit by a dramatic downturn in the second half of 1995, the Confederation of European Paper Industries (CEPI) said on Thursday.
"1996 has been a disappointing year for European producers of pulp and paper. But there is some hope for improvement," said Klaus Grewlich, director general of CEPI.
On the basis of third quarter information, Grewlich said it was possible "to indicate that the worst is probably over."
"De-stocking seems to have run its course and some grades of paper are experiencing improvements," he told the industry body's general assembly, according to a copy of his speech.
During the autumn, pulp prices were firming again and paper production and prices increased, "but probably not enough to repair the damage of the first six months," Grewlich said.
Production in the three months from July to September would be much higher than in 1995.
"There is scope for a substantial rise in the overall production figures for graphic grades," Grewlich added.
The recovery in the second half of 1996 was expected to bring the yearly figure to a production rise of between one and two percent, which Grewlich described as a cautious forecast.
This follows three straight quarters with declining production of paper and board.
After a year-on-year fall of 9.5 percent in the fourth quarter of 1995 and six percent in the first quarter of this year, output in the second quarter declined by 6.7 percent.
The fall was even more dramatic for pulp, used as raw material for paper, down 12.2 percent in the second quarter.
Grewlich said the dramatic change in the market situation for most grades of paper during the second half of 1995 with falling orders and profit margins had surprised producers.
It had also raised serious questions about developments in paper demand and supply, the role of inventories and capacity increases during volatile business cycles, he said.
The forest industry, fiercely competitive, is known for its wild business cycle swings.

This has been evident during the 1990s which started off with an economic recession in 1991-1992 following the boom of the late 1980s. The market recovered strongly in 1993 and 1994 before the new downturn which started last year.
The outlook for pulp and paper had looked good for the whole of 1995, Grewlich said, but in the summer orders evaporated and then plunged by nearly 10 percent in the final three months.

"In retrospect it became evident that part of the strong growth in 1994 and the first half of 1995 was attributable to inventory building encouraged by rising prices and concern about future availability of some grades," Grewlich said.
"By the spring and summer of 1996, companies were reporting a drastic change in profitability," he said.
This has been underlined by recent result figures.
In late October, Sweden's SCA posted a 41 percent fall in nine-month earnings and Finland's second largest forest group Enso Oy reported a 56 percent drop in its eight-month profits.

Grewlich pointed out that in the longer term paper production had increased faster than the European economy as a whole. "Thus the good news is that we can reasonably assume that the underlying growth in real demand for paper remains strong."
However, a reason for caution is the increased capacity from large new machines being built in Europe and elsewhere.
Announced expansions will increase total world capacity by eight percent, with Europe accounting for one third, he said.
